text: They are the main information stored in your `.jsonl` files. Each bullet has its own type and fields that define certain characteristics of the type
For example, a callout bullet has a *level* field that can be success, info, ...
This type of representation allows bullets to have rich and customized formatting

Basically, your bullets are stored in `.jsonl` ([JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org)) files. This means that each line of the file is a JSON object containing either a single bullet information or metadata from your notes

note: Simplified example of what a `.jsonl` file looks like in TreeWrite

text: The `.jsonl` file follows an [append-only log](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Append-only) structure. This means that adding, removing, and updating bullets or metadata never alters already written JSON objects

note: Demonstration of how the append-only log works. We write the text "Hello" in a bullet, and then update it to "Hello world". Instead of updating the existing row, we append a new duplicate row with the updated fields. From now on, only the last line is counted by TreeWrite, and the previous ones are ignored

text: All bullets have base fields (like `id` and `type`) and extra fields specific to each bullet type
Metadata is an object that contains information such as settings (favorites, tags, ...)
The reason behind this decision is very simple: ***performance***

If we were to update the bullet line with the new values, we would have to rewrite the entire file with each edit. This is because the lines don't have a fixed byte length, so we can't update a JSON object in the middle of the file without updating everything else. But appending new data to a file in the file system is a cheap and fast operation
You might be thinking that this approach would eventually leave the file huge and with a lot of old data from the same bullet, and that's true
The condition that is verified is:
In summary, the append-only log structure allows updates to your bullets to be made almost instantly, regardless of the number of bullets in your document

To resolve this, each edit validates whether the file is growing too large and should be cleaned up to contain only the most recent data. If that's the case, then the file is rewritten, now containing only the latest data
Why use a custom file format instead of a database (like SQLite)?
Some reasons to use a JSON Lines file instead of a pure JSON file:
Using an append-only log structure, each edit appends to the end of the file instead of overwriting the entire file, making TreeWrite much more performant for large documents
A damaged line or crash does not corrupt the entire document
Diffs in Git are kept small, summarized in just a few lines

text: Specific fields for each bullet type

rows: Unique identifier of the bullet, a [ULID](https://github.com/ulid/spec)
`id` of the parent bullet. Empty for bullets at the root of the document
Position of the bullet among its siblings, as a fractional index key. Siblings are sorted by it as plain strings
Type of the bullet, one of `text`, `title`, `number`, `checkbox`, `divider`, `callout`, `table`, `image`, `file`, `code`, `math` or `page`. It defines the specific fields of the bullet
Short text shown under the bullet, with inline Markdown formatting. Omitted when the bullet has no note
`id` of each tag of the bullet, as listed in the `tags` of the metadata. Omitted when the bullet has no tags
Day the bullet is about, as `YYYY-MM-DD`, or `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM` with a time of day. It has no time zone. Omitted when the bullet has no date
Whether the children of the bullet are hidden. Omitted when `false`
Always `metadata`, which tells this line apart from the bullets
Settings of the document, grouped in `theme`, `home`, `publish` and `features`
Tags of the document, in the order they are shown
`id` of each favorite bullet, in the order they are shown
Hue that tints the neutral colors (backgrounds, borders and text), an integer from `0` to `360`. Defaults to `0`
Saturation of the neutral colors, an integer from `0` to `100`. At `0` they are plain grays. Defaults to `0`
Main accent color, as a hex color like `#f21616`. Defaults to `#f21616`
Second accent color, as a hex color. Defaults to `#ffa903`
Third accent color, as a hex color. Defaults to `#605cac`

Address of the published site, an `http` or `https` URL ending in a slash
Shell command that publishes the built site. Empty or omitted to only build it. Never included in the published site
Sidebar features turned off, any of `pathway`, `favorites`, `tags`, `calendar` and `assets`. Omitted when all are on
Unique identifier of the tag, a ULID, which bullets list in their `tags`
Name of the tag, up to 40 characters and unique regardless of case
Color of the tag, as a hex color. Omitted to show the tag in a dimmed color
Whether the Git integration is on. Defaults to `false`
`sync` pulls the changes of other machines before pushing, and `backup` only pushes. Defaults to `sync`
Minutes after the last change before the document is committed and synced, from `0.5` to `1440`. Defaults to `1`
Minutes between pulls of the changes of other machines, even with nothing changed locally, from `0.5` to `1440`. Defaults to `5`
Whether changes are pulled when the document is opened. Defaults to `true`
Template of the commit messages, which takes `{{file}}`, `{{date}}` and `{{hostname}}`. Defaults to `{{file}} from {{hostname}} at {{date}}`
